extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of aesthetics, philosophers of art, and creative artists seeking principles for beauty and form
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical/aesthetic principles and evaluative criteria about beauty, appearance, form, and the moral/social role of taste — intended to guide judgment of art, manners, and aesthetic development. Emphasizes the relation of feeling and thought, independence of appearance, and conditions in which aesthetic sense flourishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as union of form and life
rubrics_metrics.description: "Beauty is therefore doubtless form, because we contemplate it, but it is equally life because we feel it. In a word, it is at once our state and our act."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective beauty blends reflection (form, contemplation) and feeling (life, sensation) so that the transition from active to passive is not perceived; aesthetic judgment should treat form and feeling reciprocally as cause and effect. Anti-pattern: treating beauty as purely intellectual abstraction or purely sensory pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance must be frank and independent to be aesthetical
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is only by being frank or disclaiming all reality, and by being independent or doing without reality, that the appearance is aesthetical."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic appearance must not ape reality or rely on reality for effect. If appearance needs reality for its effect it becomes a mere instrument for material ends. Example contrast: a beautiful painted woman pleases as independent appearance; a living woman pleases for other reasons and may not evoke the pure aesthetic feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let the ideal usurp reality (poetic boundary)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The poet transgresses his proper limits when he attributes being to his ideal... or else he renounces his right as a poet by letting experience encroach on the sphere of the ideal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators should preserve the boundary between ideal (aesthetic possibility) and real experience: do not present the ideal as a determined factual existence, nor let empirical constraints wholly govern the ideal. Anti-patterns: conflating utopian ideals with facts; grounding art solely in empirical literalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict separation of form from substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Success in extending the empire of the beautiful depends on "the strictness with which he separates form from substance: for if he frees appearance from reality, he must also do the converse."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate and value form for its own sake and be able to distinguish formal appearance from material content. Artistic judgment should reward clarity in formal shaping irrespective of mere material use. Anti-pattern: letting material utility subsume formal considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic play requires a legislative/unifying mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The aesthetic play occurs when "the legislative mind is mixed with the acts of a blind instinct, subjects the arbitrary march of the imagination to its eternal and immutable unity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True aesthetic play is not random association; it requires ordering intelligence that gives unity and permanence to imaginative material. Early or uncultivated taste that prefers grotesque, violent, or disordered novelty indicates absence of this unifying control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progression from material play to aesthetic play
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagination "from this play of free association of ideas... by making the attempt of creating a free form, passes at length at a jump to the aesthetic play."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic maturity involves moving from mere exuberant/aimless fancy to purposeful formal creation — ornamentation, measured song, harmonious movement. Indicators of progress: work reflects deliberate form, restraint, and harmony rather than only stimulus or shock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for form over substance as sign of cultural humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: "As soon as he begins to prefer form to substance and to risk reality for appearance... the barriers of animal life fall, and he finds himself on a track that has no end."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuing the superfluous (ornament, fashion, play) beyond immediate needs signals developed aesthetic sensibility. In evaluation, the willingness to sacrifice mere utility for formal richness marks aesthetic advancement. Anti-pattern: judging all ornament as frivolous without appreciating formal enrichment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of appearance (dress, games) signals aesthetic initiation
rubrics_metrics.description: "The love of appearance, the inclination for dress and for games" accompanies the initiation of the savage into humanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signposts of emerging aesthetic culture include attention to appearance, play, and imitative/formal arts. Critics should treat such signs as positive indicators of aesthetic development rather than mere vanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance as play, not deception
rubrics_metrics.description: "If it is liked it is because it is an appearance, and not because it is held to be something better than it is: the first principle alone is a play, whilst the second is a deception."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate appearance positively when it is enjoyed as appearance (play, imaginative value). When appearance tries to masquerade as reality (deception), it becomes ethically and aesthetically suspect. Distinguish 'needy appearance' (seeking to replace reality) from independent aesthetic appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic appearance cannot endanger moral truth
rubrics_metrics.description: "The aesthetical appearance can never endanger the truth of morals: wherever it seems to do so the appearance is not aesthetical."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an appearance undermines moral truth; if it does, it fails the test of genuine aesthetic appearance. Examples of failure: duplicity, paltry semblance used to mask lack of substance or moral unworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste mediates and unites individual and communal experience
rubrics_metrics.description: "Taste alone brings harmony into society, because it creates harmony in the individual... Beauty alone can we enjoy both as individuals and as a race."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art and aesthetic judgment should aim for universality—forms that can be enjoyed both personally and communally. Successful aesthetic works enable shared pleasure and common-sense comprehension rather than exclusive erudition; genius must make itself familiar to a broad audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic cultivation needs particular social/environmental conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: "The germ of the beautiful will find an equal difficulty in developing itself in countries where a severe nature forbids man to enjoy himself, and in those where a prodigal nature dispenses him from all effort... It will only flourish in places where man converses peacefully with himself in his cottage, and with the whole race when he issues from it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating cultural output or planning artistic communities, consider whether conditions (leisure, sociability, supportive climate) permit aesthetic sensibility to develop. Anti-cases: extreme deprivation, harsh survival, nomadic anonymity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament and craftsmanship signal aesthetic maturity
rubrics_metrics.description: "The object ought also to reflect the enlightened intelligence which imagines it, the hand which shaped it with affection, the mind free and serene which chose it and exposed it to view."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value craftsmanship and visible care in objects (furniture, clothing, tools). Evaluation should reward works where utility is accompanied by evident shaping intelligence and affectionate making. Anti-pattern: dismissing all functional objects when they bear aesthetic care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste is morally beneficial but not a substitute for morality
rubrics_metrics.description: "A strong and pure feeling for the beautiful ought to exercise a salutary influence upon the moral life... alone, and by its unaided influence, it could never produce anything moral."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In judging character or practices, recognize that aesthetic sensibility can encourage moral dispositions (restraint, generosity) but cannot replace ethical principles. Do not conflate elegance with goodness; test actions by moral standards as well as taste.
